title: Prototype systems for rechargeable magnesium batteries
section: 1.1. Why magnesium needs its own electrolyte logic
text: A magnesium-metal electrolyte must deliver species that rearrange their ligands, accept electrons and join the metal as the surface evolves. The early rechargeable prototype paired an organohaloaluminate electrolyte with a Chevrel-phase cathode.[1,2,3] Subsequent work established the importance of both liquid chemistry and surface preparation.[4,5] These constraints remain central to magnesium and other multivalent batteries.[6,7,8,9] We ask how a working formulation supplies magnesium, and which part of that explanation can guide another formulation.

title: Nonaqueous Liquid Electrolytes for Lithium-Based Rechargeable Batteries
section: 1.1. Why magnesium needs its own electrolyte logic
text: Lithium provides a useful comparison, but its interphase logic is insufficient for magnesium. title: Organic Electrolyte Design for Rechargeable Batteries: From Lithium to Magnesium
section: 1.1. Why magnesium needs its own electrolyte logic
text: Mg²⁺ generally binds more strongly than Li⁺ to comparable donors, with ligand denticity, association and polarization reshaping its coordination.[21,22] Here, denticity means the number of donor atoms from one ligand that bind the metal. Anion binding changes the complex charge and geometry, while the metal remains formally Mg(II) until reduction. The reacting species may differ from the dominant bulk solvate. The apparent paradox follows: reasoning from film formation encourages anion participation; reasoning from persistent binding encourages exclusion. Both directions have produced working electrolytes.[23,24] Identifying the reaction affected by each resolves the contradiction.

section: 1.2. A working recipe needs a reaction mechanism
text: A favourable recipe does not identify its mechanism. Coordination number and isolated binding energy describe parts of the liquid, but do not identify the slow transfer step.[22,29,30] Chloride calculations illustrate the distinction: one computational comparison found easier desolvation from clusters alongside more difficult electron transfer.[31,32] This is a system-dependent result, not an experimentally established rule that aggregation always accelerates exchange. title: Solvent–Anion Counterpoised Electrolyte Enables High‐Rate Magnesium Metal Batteries
section: 1.3. Our position and the criterion for progress
text: We propose choosing a first-shell anion for its effect on magnesium transfer. Binding may replace a persistent solvent donor, redistribute electron density and change the geometry through which remaining ligands depart. These effects can precede film formation. Studies of competing solvent–anion interactions, dynamic solvation and changes outside the primary shell motivate this view.[24,37,38] We distinguish direct anion coordination, meaning a Mg–anion donor contact, from the broader term ion association. A contact ion pair has such a contact; a solvent-separated pair has intervening solvent. Neither pairing nor dissociation implies a bare Mg²⁺ ion in solution.

section: 6.3. Engineer pathways that remain useful in a cell
text: The decisive test uses the same electrolyte at both electrodes with limited metal and liquid inventories.[142,6] A molecular advantage must survive cathode exposure, surface evolution and repeated transfer without unacceptable loss. Identifying the populated carrier, productive reaction and chemical fate connects coordination to that test.
